title: AlphaZero
subtitle: Self-play, tree search and learning without human knowledge
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A 12-chapter course on AlphaZero, the DeepMind algorithm that learns chess, shogi and Go from self-play with only the rules. Based on the AlphaZero preprint and Science paper by Silver and colleagues, the AlphaGo Zero Nature paper and reports on the matches and the debate that followed. Covers game search, Monte Carlo tree search, the policy and value network, PUCT, exploration noise and temperature, self-play data, the loss and training, differences from AlphaGo Zero, results and criticism, a working tic-tac-toe search and successors such as MuZero. Python labs run on the built-in MicroPython engine. The original program was never released; the capstone is a teaching miniature.

summary: AlphaZero is a reinforcement learning algorithm from DeepMind that learns board games from scratch. It starts from random play and is given nothing but the rules. It plays against itself, and in its first paper it reached superhuman strength in chess, shogi and Go.

Its core is a loop. A neural network guides a Monte Carlo tree search. The search picks moves and plays games against itself. The finished games become training data that improve the network, which makes the next search better.
The course builds every piece in small Python programs: game search, tree search, the network's outputs, the loss, the training loop and a tiny working search for tic-tac-toe.

items: ELI5. AlphaZero learns chess, shogi and Go from nothing but the rules. It plays itself, notices what wins, and improves. Like a child who learns a game by playing a thousand times and never reading a book.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what does AlphaZero know at the start, and what does it learn?
AlphaZero is a reinforcement learning algorithm published by DeepMind in a preprint in December 2017, with a peer-reviewed version in the journal Science on 7 December 2018.

Its abstract claims that, starting from random play and given no domain knowledge except the game rules, it reached superhuman play in chess and shogi as well as Go within 24 hours, and convincingly defeated a world-champion program in each.

To see why that mattered, look at what came before. The strongest chess and shogi programs used a highly optimized alpha-beta search with many domain-specific adaptations, and an evaluation function written by human experts over decades.
AlphaZero replaces the handwritten evaluation and move-ordering rules with a deep neural network, and replaces alpha-beta with a general-purpose Monte Carlo tree search.

The line of programs. AlphaGo Fan beat the European Go champion Fan Hui in October 2015. AlphaGo Lee beat Lee Sedol in March 2016. AlphaGo Master then beat a team of professionals online. These versions all started from supervised learning on human expert games.
AlphaGo Zero, published in Nature in October 2017, removed the human data completely and learned Go from self-play alone; it beat the earlier champion-defeating AlphaGo 100 games to 0.

AlphaZero is the next step: a more generic version of AlphaGo Zero. It drops Go-specific details such as symmetry augmentation and the gating of new networks, and applies the same algorithm to chess and shogi, whose rules are asymmetric and whose moves are harder to encode.
The only game-specific setting that changed between games was the scale of the exploration noise.

The heart of it is one function. A neural network f with parameters theta takes a board position s and returns a vector p of move probabilities and a scalar v, the expected outcome of the game for the player to move. Early in training the outputs are close to random.
Everything else in the algorithm exists to make them good.

The loop has three steps that repeat. First, play: at every position, run a tree search that uses the network, choose a move from the search result, and play a whole game against yourself. Second, record: for each position keep the search's move probabilities and the final outcome.
Third, train: adjust the network so that p matches the search probabilities and v matches the outcomes. Then play again with the improved network.

A useful way to see it, used in the papers: the search acts as a policy improvement step, since it produces better move probabilities than the raw network gives, and the network is trained toward them. Self-play outcomes act as policy evaluation. Chapter 8 returns to this.

A note on sources. This course follows the AlphaZero preprint and Science paper by Silver and colleagues, the AlphaGo Zero paper in Nature, and secondary coverage of the matches and the debate that followed. Numbers quoted come from those sources.
Chapter 11 is my own tic-tac-toe implementation, a small demonstration of the idea and not a copy of DeepMind's code, which was never released.
Be realistic about scale. The published training used thousands of specialized chips. The labs here are tiny versions that teach the mechanics; they are not meant to reach master strength.

summary: The games AlphaZero plays are two-player, zero-sum, perfect-information games: players alternate, one's gain is the other's loss, and nothing is hidden. They can be drawn as a game tree whose root is the current position and whose edges are legal moves.

Minimax searches the tree assuming both sides play best. Negamax is the same idea written with one function by flipping the sign at each level. Alpha-beta pruning skips branches that cannot change the result.

Full trees are far too big for chess, so classical engines search to a limited depth and score the leaves with a handwritten evaluation function. Replacing that function with a learned one is the main idea AlphaZero builds on.

items: ELI5. Classical chess engines look at millions of positions per second and use rules written by humans. They are fast calculators with human advice. AlphaZero swaps the advice for what it learns.
Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: how do classical engines differ from AlphaZero?

Before AlphaZero's own ideas, we need the vocabulary of game search. The papers apply to games with two players who alternate moves, where one player's win is the other's loss and the full position is visible to both. Chess, shogi and Go all fit. Poker, with hidden cards, does not.

A game tree has the current position at its root, one child for each legal move, and so on until positions where the game is over. Each finished position has a result, win, draw or loss. For tic-tac-toe the tree is small enough to search completely. For chess it is astronomically large.
Minimax gives each position a value, assuming that both players choose the best option. The player to move picks the child with the best value for themselves.

Negamax is the compact way to write it, using the fact that the game is zero-sum: the value of a position for the player to move is the best, over all moves, of the negative of the child's value, because the child is seen from the opponent's side.

lesson.tex: \begin{gathered} V(s) = \max_{a}\,\bigl(-V(s')\bigr), \\[0.6em] s' = \text{result of move } a \text{ in } s \end{gathered}

items: At a finished position the value is plus one if the player to move has won, minus one if they have lost and zero for a draw. In practice the player to move has always just been beaten when a game ends by a completed line, so the value there is minus one.

Alpha-beta pruning keeps two numbers, the best value already guaranteed to the player to move and to the opponent, and stops looking at a branch once it cannot matter. The result is exactly the minimax value, but far fewer nodes are visited when good moves are tried first.
Chess engines add move-ordering rules, transposition tables, search extensions, opening books, endgame tablebases and many other devices.
Even so, nobody can search chess to the end. Engines stop at a depth and call an evaluation function, a formula written by humans from features such as material, king safety and pawn structure.
The AlphaZero paper describes Stockfish this way, and notes that other strong programs, including Deep Blue, use very similar architectures.
Stockfish itself later added a small neural network evaluation, so today's classical engines blur the line; the 2017 contrast was between handwritten and learned knowledge.

Shogi, Japanese chess, is harder for such methods than chess: it is played on a larger board, and a captured piece changes sides and may be dropped almost anywhere. Go, with its large branching factor and hard-to-score positions, resisted classical search for even longer.
The question AlphaZero asks is whether one method can handle all three without handwritten knowledge.

The practice section implements the fundamentals on tic-tac-toe: detect a winner, compute negamax values, and count how many nodes minimax and alpha-beta visit. Boards are strings of nine characters, X, O or a dot for empty, read row by row.

summary: Monte Carlo tree search grows a tree one simulation at a time. Each simulation walks down the tree choosing promising moves, adds a new node, evaluates it and passes the result back up. Over many simulations the statistics at the root point to the best move.
The classic choice rule comes from multi-armed bandits: try moves with a high average reward, but also moves tried rarely. UCB1 adds an exploration bonus that shrinks as a move is visited more.
Classic MCTS evaluates a new node by playing random moves to the end of the game. AlphaZero keeps the same four phases but replaces the random rollout with the network's value.

items: ELI5. Monte Carlo tree search builds a tree of moves by trying ideas, scoring them and returning to the promising ones. Like exploring a maze: you walk down a path, note how it went, and next time take better turns.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what are the four steps of one search iteration?

Alpha-beta search looks at every move to a fixed depth. Monte Carlo tree search instead grows a tree unevenly, spending most effort on promising lines. It needs no handwritten evaluation, only the rules, which is why it suited Go, where good evaluation functions were hard to write.

Each node of the tree is a position, and each edge a move. For every edge we keep a visit count and a total value. One simulation has four phases. Selection: starting at the root, repeatedly choose a child by a rule until reaching a position not yet in the tree. Expansion: add that position.
Evaluation: estimate how good it is. Backup: walk back up the path and update the counts and values of every edge used.

The question is how to choose in selection. This is the multi-armed bandit problem: several slot machines with unknown payoffs. You want to pull the best one, but you only learn about each by pulling it. Pure greed can get stuck on a mediocre option that happened to pay early.
Pure exploration wastes pulls.

The UCB1 rule picks the option with the highest score. W over N is the average reward so far of option a, which favours good options. The second term is a bonus that is large for options with few visits and shrinks as they are tried, which favours exploring.
N is the total number of pulls and c sets how adventurous the search is. Applied to the edges at each tree node this gives the UCT algorithm, due to Kocsis and Szepesvári.

Classic MCTS evaluates a newly added position by a rollout: play random moves to the end and note who won. One rollout is a noisy estimate, but averaged over thousands it is informative. Go programs built on this approach reached strong amateur level before neural networks.

The final move is chosen from the root's statistics. Usually the most visited move is chosen, not the one with the best average, because visit counts are more robust. A move with a great average after two visits is probably luck.

What AlphaZero changes: the rollout is replaced by the network's value estimate, and the UCB rule is replaced by a variant that also uses the network's move probabilities as a prior. The structure of four phases stays the same. Chapter 5 gives the exact rule.
In the practice section you compute the UCB1 score and write the selection step.

summary: AlphaZero's network takes a board position and returns two things: a probability for every possible move (the policy) and one number estimating the outcome (the value). One shared body of convolutional layers feeds two output heads.

The policy is produced with a softmax over all moves, then illegal moves are zeroed out and the rest renormalized. For chess, moves are encoded as 73 planes of 8 by 8 squares: for each from-square, 56 queen-style moves, 8 knight moves and 9 underpromotions.
Early in training the network knows nothing, so p is nearly uniform and v is near zero. Everything it later knows comes from self-play.

items: ELI5. One network with two heads looks at the board. One head says which moves look good, the other says who is winning. It is a coach whispering a hunch and a score.
Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what are the two outputs of the network?

The learned part of AlphaZero is a single neural network f with parameters theta. It takes a position and returns a pair: a vector p giving a probability for each move, and a scalar v estimating the expected outcome.
The papers describe the body as many residual blocks of convolutional layers with batch normalization and rectifier non-linearities, followed by two small output heads.
The value v is a number between minus one and plus one, from the point of view of the player to move. A value near plus one means a likely win, near minus one a likely loss.
Unlike AlphaGo Zero, which assumed only win or loss, AlphaZero estimates the expected outcome, which also covers draws, an important thing in chess where most top games are drawn.

Turning scores into a policy. The last layer of the policy head produces one raw score per possible move. A softmax makes them positive and sums them to one. It subtracts the largest score first for numerical stability, which does not change the result.

Most possible moves are illegal in any given position. So the policy is masked: probabilities of illegal moves are set to zero and the remainder renormalized to sum to one. If every legal move happens to have zero probability, a sensible fallback is to spread probability evenly over the legal moves.

Representing chess. The paper's input is a stack of 8 by 8 planes. It holds piece positions for each side over the last eight positions, plus constant planes for the side to move, the move count, castling rights and the no-progress counter, 119 planes in total. The output is 8 by 8 by 73.
Each square of the grid marks the square a piece moves from, and the 73 planes say how it moves.

Of the 73 planes, 56 are queen-style moves: eight compass directions times seven distances. Eight are knight moves. Nine are underpromotions, a pawn moving or capturing to a knight, bishop or rook. That gives 8 times 8 times 73, which is 4,672 move slots.
Promotions to a queen are encoded as ordinary queen-style moves.

For shogi and Go the encodings differ, but the principle is the same: the game rules supply the board and a fixed catalogue of moves, and the network learns everything else. This is why the algorithm is general: only the encoding of positions and moves is game-specific.

In the practice section you implement the softmax, the legal-move mask, and the queen-move plane numbering. The compass order used in the lab is my own convention; the paper does not fix an order in its text.

chapters.title: MCTS guided by the network (PUCT)

maps.title: AlphaZero's search
links: Edge | stores | N, W, Q and P

summary: Each edge of the search tree stores a visit count N, a total value W, a mean value Q equal to W over N, and a prior probability P from the network. Selection picks the edge with the largest Q plus U, where U is an exploration bonus proportional to the prior and shrinking with visits.

When a simulation reaches a leaf, the network evaluates it. Its policy becomes the priors of the new edges and its value is backed up along the path, with the sign flipped at every level since the players alternate. No random rollout is used.
After many simulations the root visit counts form a probability distribution over moves. That distribution is the search's answer, and it is also the training target for the policy.

glossary.def: For each move from a position: visit count N, total value W, mean value Q = W/N, prior P.
Polynomial upper confidence trees: the selection rule Q + c * P * sqrt(sum N) / (1 + N).
The network's probability for a move, used to guide search before the move has been tried.
Creating the edges for a new position, with priors from the network.
Updating counts and values along the path from leaf to root.
The distribution over root moves given by visit counts.

keyPoints: Selection: a = argmax over moves of Q(s,a) + U(s,a).
U(s,a) = c * P(s,a) * sqrt(sum_b N(s,b)) / (1 + N(s,a)).
Leaf: (p, v) = f(s); store p as priors, back up v.
Backup: N += 1, W += v, Q = W / N, with the sign flipped at each level.
In the AlphaZero pseudocode c is c_init + log((1 + N + c_base) / c_base), with c_init = 1.25 and c_base = 19652.
Training used 800 simulations per move.

items: ELI5. PUCT is the rule for picking which move to explore: a mix of how well it has done, how promising the network thinks it is, and how little it has been tried. Like choosing which restaurant to try again.
Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what three things does the PUCT score balance?
Chapter 3 described MCTS with UCB1 and random rollouts. AlphaZero keeps the four phases but changes both ingredients. Let us look at the tree.

For every position s in the tree and every legal move a, there is an edge storing four numbers: a visit count N, a total value W, a mean value Q equal to W divided by N, and a prior probability P that came from the network when the position was first expanded.

Selection. Starting at the root, each simulation picks, at every position, the edge that maximizes Q plus U. The exploration term U is proportional to the prior, grows with the total number of visits to the position, and shrinks as the edge itself is visited. This follows the AlphaGo Zero paper.

Look at the behaviour. Early in the search all N are zero, so Q is taken as zero and moves are chosen by the prior alone: the network's favourites are tried first. As a move is visited its bonus falls, and moves with lower priors but good values start to win. Moves with high Q keep being visited.
In the long run the visit counts concentrate on the best moves.

Expansion and evaluation. When the walk reaches a position that is not yet in the tree, the network is called once on it. It returns p and v. The vector p, masked to the legal moves, gives the priors of the new edges. The scalar v is the value of the position for the player to move.
There is no rollout to the end of the game.

Backup, with a subtlety. Every edge's Q is from the point of view of the player who chooses that move. The value v belongs to the player to move at the leaf, who is the opponent of the player who chose the last edge.
So the last edge receives minus v, the one above it plus v, and so on, alternating up to the root. Each edge on the path also gets N plus one.

The AlphaZero paper does not print the exploration formula in its main text, and the later pseudocode makes the constant depend on the visit count of the position: log of one plus N plus c_base over c_base, plus c_init, with c_init equal to 1.25 and c_base equal to 19652.

The constant grows very slowly with visits. The papers give no experiments on this choice, and the reason for modifying the formula was not discussed. The version in the lab is the simple AlphaGo Zero form.

Choosing the move. After the simulations, the search returns a probability distribution based on root visit counts. In training, moves are chosen in proportion to those counts. In evaluation, the program picks the most-visited move. During training each search used 800 simulations.

Cost and speed. The papers report AlphaZero searching about 80 thousand positions per second in chess, 40 thousand in shogi and 16 thousand in Go. Stockfish searched about 70 million per second, and the shogi program Elmo about 35 million.
AlphaZero examines roughly a thousand times fewer positions, but each is judged by a much better evaluator. In the practice section you will implement the score, the selection and the backup.

summary: If a program always plays its single best move, it may play the same game forever and learn nothing new. AlphaZero adds randomness in two places: noise on the root priors, and sampling the played move from the visit counts.

The Dirichlet noise mixes a random probability vector into the network's priors at the root. Its concentration is scaled inversely to the typical number of legal moves: 0.3 for chess, 0.15 for shogi, 0.03 for Go. This was the only game-specific hyperparameter.

Temperature controls how sharply the visit counts are turned into move probabilities. At temperature one, moves are chosen in proportion to visits. As it approaches zero, the most-visited move is always chosen.

items: ELI5. To keep learning, the program must sometimes try odd moves. Noise at the root adds surprise, and temperature controls how boldly it picks. Without it, it would repeat its own habits forever.
Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: why add noise and temperature during self-play?

Self-play only teaches the program something if the games vary. A program that always plays its best-looking move, from the same start, would repeat one game. So AlphaZero deliberately injects randomness, in two places.

The first place is the root of each search. Dirichlet noise is added to the network's prior probabilities at the root, so moves the network currently dislikes still get tried. The mix is a weighted average of the network's prior and a random vector eta drawn from a Dirichlet distribution.
AlphaGo Zero used epsilon equal to 0.25; the AlphaZero paper does not state epsilon in its main text.

What the Dirichlet distribution does. It produces random vectors of non-negative numbers summing to one. With a small concentration alpha the vectors are spiky: most mass sits on a few moves, chosen at random.

That is what you want, since a good surprise is usually one specific alternative, not a faint boost for everything. The AlphaZero paper scales alpha inversely to the typical number of legal moves: 0.3 for chess, 0.15 for shogi and 0.03 for Go. Go has the most legal moves and gets the smallest alpha.

The second place is the move actually played. After the search, the root visit counts N are turned into a distribution with a temperature tau. The probability of a move is proportional to its visit count raised to the power one over tau. At tau equal to one this is plain proportion to visits.
As tau goes toward zero the largest count takes everything, so the most-visited move is chosen.
AlphaGo Zero used tau equal to one for the first 30 moves of each game, so openings vary, and then almost zero, so later play is sharp.

The AlphaZero paper describes moves chosen in proportion to root visit counts during training and greedily in evaluation, without printing a temperature schedule in its main text. Both settings are therefore described here as AlphaGo Zero's.
Two clarifications. First, the temperature affects only which real move is played in the game. Inside a search, the tree is still walked by the PUCT rule.
Second, the training target for the policy is the visit distribution, not the move that was played, so the occasional exploratory move does not teach the network to play badly.
In the practice section you turn visit counts into a policy at a given temperature, mix noise into priors, set the schedule, and sample from a distribution given a random number.

summary: A self-play game gives one training example per position played: the position s, the search probabilities pi that were used to choose the move, and the final outcome z of the game. The outcome is the same game result, but seen from the side of whoever was to move in that position.
So if the first player wins, z is plus one for every position where the first player was to move and minus one for the others. A draw gives zero for all.
Go has eightfold symmetry, which AlphaGo Zero used to multiply its data. Chess and shogi are not symmetric, so AlphaZero does not augment its data or transform positions during search.

items: ELI5. Each self-played game becomes homework: the positions, what the search decided, and who won. The network studies these examples and gets better, then plays better games. A loop that lifts itself.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what three things are stored for each training position?

What does a game of self-play teach? Each game is a sequence of positions s1, s2, up to a final position sT. At every position the program ran a search and played a move. After the game ends, the rules say who won. The program then writes one record for every position played.

A record has three parts. The position s_t, in the network's input encoding. The search probabilities pi_t, the distribution over moves produced by the tree search at that position. And the outcome z_t.
The value z is plus one if the player to move at position t went on to win, minus one if they went on to lose, and zero for a draw.

lesson.tex: z_t = \begin{cases} +1 & \text{player to move at } t \text{ wins} \\ 0 & \text{draw} \\ -1 & \text{player to move at } t \text{ loses} \end{cases}

items: An example. Suppose a game lasts five moves and the first player wins. The first player moved at moves one, three and five; they get z equal to plus one for those positions. The second player moved at positions two and four, and gets minus one.
Note that the same game result is seen from alternating sides, which matches the network's value being defined for the player to move.

Where the target pi comes from matters. It is the visit distribution from the search, not the move chosen. Because moves early in a game are sampled randomly in proportion to visits, the move played is a noisy sample, while pi is the search's whole opinion.
Training the policy toward pi teaches the network to predict what a better search would conclude.

Where the game ends. The rules decide: checkmate, stalemate or other draws in chess, for example. AlphaGo Zero ended Go games when both players passed or after 19 times 19 times 2, which is 722, moves, and scored by Tromp-Taylor rules.
In AlphaZero the outcome may be a draw, which matters for chess: it optimizes the expected outcome, not just the chance of winning.

Symmetry. Go positions have eight symmetries: four rotations, each with or without a reflection. AlphaGo Zero used these, for example by feeding the network a random transform of the board during training and search.
The rules of chess and shogi are asymmetric, and so AlphaZero does not augment the training data and does not transform the board during MCTS.

Where the data goes. Self-play games are generated continuously by many workers; the training process samples mini-batches of positions from recent games. In the published AlphaZero runs, self-play used 5,000 first-generation TPUs while 64 second-generation TPUs trained the network.
In the practice section you build the outcome list for a game, form the training triples, and count the distinct symmetric copies of a tic-tac-toe board.

summary: The network is trained on the self-play records to make two predictions: the value v should match the game outcome z, and the policy p should match the search probabilities pi. A third term penalizes large weights.
The loss is the sum of a squared error on the value, a cross-entropy between pi and p, and an L2 regularization term. It is minimized with mini-batch gradient descent on batches of positions.
This works as policy iteration. The search improves on the raw policy, the network is trained to imitate the improved policy, and the improved network makes the next search stronger.

glossary.def: A number that measures the network's error; training lowers it.
The average of squared differences, used for the value.
-sum pi log p: how well p matches the target distribution pi.
A penalty c times the squared size of the weights.
A small random sample of training positions used for one gradient step.
The size of each update step; AlphaZero lowered it in stages.
A measure of how different two distributions are; cross-entropy minus entropy.

keyPoints: l = (z - v)^2 - pi . log p + c ||theta||^2.
The value target z is -1, 0 or +1.
The policy target pi is the MCTS visit distribution.
AlphaZero used mini-batches of 4,096 positions for 700 thousand steps.
The learning rate was 0.2, dropped to 0.02, then 0.002, then 0.0002.
Search = policy improvement; game outcome = policy evaluation.

items: ELI5. The loss asks the network to match two things: the search's stronger move choice, and the actual game result. Like a student checking answers against both the teacher's notes and the final exam.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: which two targets does the training loss compare to?

The records from chapter 7 are the training data. For each position s, the network gives p and v. We want v close to the outcome z, and p close to the search distribution pi. One number combines these goals, the loss.

The first term is a squared error on the value: if the network said minus one for a position whose game was won, the error is large. The second term is the cross-entropy between the search distribution pi and the network's p, a sum over moves of minus pi times the logarithm of p.
It is smallest when p equals pi. The third term is a penalty on the size of the weights controlled by a constant c, a standard guard against overfitting.
Cross-entropy is related to a distance between distributions. The cross-entropy of pi against p equals the entropy of pi plus the KL divergence from pi to p.
The entropy of pi does not depend on the network, so minimizing the cross-entropy is the same as minimizing the KL divergence: pulling p toward pi.

Gradient descent. The loss is averaged over a mini-batch of positions sampled from self-play data, and the parameters theta take a step against the gradient, scaled by the learning rate. AlphaZero's published runs used 700 thousand mini-batches of 4,096 positions.
The learning rate started at 0.2 and was dropped to 0.02, then 0.002 and finally 0.0002. The same network and settings were used for all three games.

Why does this work at all? The viewpoint in the papers is policy iteration. The raw network policy is a guess. Searching with the network gives a better policy, because the search looks ahead and corrects the network's mistakes with real game continuations.

The network is trained toward that better policy, which improves it. This is policy improvement. The game outcomes, in turn, show how good the play really was, and so train the value, which is policy evaluation.

Bootstrapping. At first the network is random, so the search is only slightly better than random, and its games are noisy. But the outcomes of games are real facts decided by the rules, so even random play carries signal: positions leading to wins are given higher values.
Gradually the value estimates improve, the search improves, and so on.

A note of caution from the literature. Later research observed that neither AlphaZero nor MuZero guarantees policy improvement unless all actions are evaluated at the root, and proposed Gumbel-based variants that do.
So the improvement picture is a good intuition, not a theorem about the original algorithm.

summary: AlphaZero is described in its paper as a more generic version of AlphaGo Zero. It differs in several places. Gone is the evaluation step in which a newly trained network had to beat the best player by a 55 percent margin before it could generate self-play games.

Instead a single network is updated continually and always generates the games. AlphaZero also optimizes the expected outcome including draws, uses no symmetry augmentation, and uses the same hyperparameters across games without per-game tuning, except for the exploration noise.
The published training used thousands of first-generation TPUs for self-play and 64 second-generation TPUs for learning. The training lasted 9, 12 and 34 hours for chess, shogi and Go.

items: ELI5. AlphaGo Zero dropped human games; AlphaZero then dropped Go-specific tricks. Each step removed a crutch. The result is one general recipe for many board games.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what did each generation remove from the previous one?
AlphaZero grew out of AlphaGo Zero, and the AlphaZero paper lists the differences with care. They show which parts of the earlier design were Go-specific or only precautions.

Difference one: gating. In AlphaGo Zero, self-play games were generated by the best player found so far. After each training iteration, the new network was played against the best one, and only if it won by a margin of 55 percent did it replace it. In AlphaZero this evaluation step is removed.

A single network is updated continually, and self-play always uses its latest parameters. This is simpler and removes a source of delay, at the cost of possibly using a slightly worse network for a while.

Difference two: the target. AlphaGo Zero estimated and optimized the probability of winning, assuming outcomes are win or loss. AlphaZero estimates and optimizes the expected outcome, taking account of draws or other outcomes.
That fits chess, where draws are common and an important part of the game.

Difference three: symmetry. Go is invariant to rotation and reflection, and AlphaGo Zero used that to augment training data and to transform positions during the search. The rules of chess and shogi are asymmetric, so AlphaZero does neither.

Difference four: tuning. AlphaGo Zero tuned its search hyperparameters by Bayesian optimization. AlphaZero reuses the same hyperparameters and network architecture across games, with only the Dirichlet noise scaled in inverse proportion to the typical number of legal moves.

What stayed the same: a deep network giving a policy and a value, Monte Carlo tree search with the same selection logic, self-play from random initial parameters, and the loss function of chapter 8. In that sense the algorithm is general because it was already mostly game-independent.
Scale. The paper reports 700 thousand training steps with mini-batches of 4,096 positions. Self-play used 5,000 first-generation TPUs and training used 64 second-generation TPUs.
The games generated were 44 million for chess, 24 million for shogi and 21 million for Go, taking about 9, 12 and 34 hours. Each move was chosen after 800 simulations in training.

A note on what AlphaGo Zero's own numbers were. Its Nature paper reports about three days of training from random play, 4.9 million self-play games, 1,600 simulations per move, which is roughly 0.4 seconds of thinking per move, and a 100 to 0 win over the AlphaGo version that had beaten Lee Sedol.
Different networks and hardware were used for the two programs, so the sizes are not directly comparable.

summary: In the 2017 preprint AlphaZero played a 100-game match against Stockfish 8 and scored 28 wins, 72 draws and no losses. It also beat Elmo in shogi and a 3-day AlphaGo Zero in Go.
The result was criticized for the settings: Stockfish had 64 threads and only 1 GB of hash memory, one minute per move, and no opening book or tablebases.

The Science paper in 2018 reported a new 1000-game match under tournament-style conditions, 3 hours plus 15 seconds per move with 44 threads, 32 GB hash and tablebases, against a Stockfish 9 development version: 155 wins, 839 draws and 6 losses. AlphaZero ran on four TPUs and a 44-core CPU.

items: ELI5. Elo measures how often you beat another player. AlphaZero beat top engines after hours of training. People argue about hardware and match conditions, so read the claim carefully.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what does the debate about the results question?

What did AlphaZero actually achieve? The first paper reports 100-game matches against a world-champion program in each game, and time to reach those levels. We will go through the numbers, then the controversy.

Chess. Against Stockfish 8, the 2016 TCEC champion, with one minute per move, AlphaZero scored 25 wins and 25 draws as White and 3 wins and 47 draws as Black, with no losses: 28 wins, 72 draws, 0 losses in 100 games. Stockfish 8 and Elmo were run with 64 threads and 1 gigabyte of hash.
AlphaZero is reported to have matched Stockfish's strength after about 4 hours of training.

Shogi. Against Elmo, the 2017 champion of the Computer Shogi Association, AlphaZero played two sets of 50 games, one for each colour, winning 43, drawing 2 and losing 5 in one and winning 47 and losing 3 in the other, and passed Elmo in under two hours of training. Go.
Against the 3-day version of AlphaGo Zero, AlphaZero won 31 of 50 games and 29 of 50 in the two colour assignments, passing AlphaGo Lee in about 8 hours.

The engines searched very differently. AlphaZero examined about 80 thousand positions per second in chess, 40 thousand in shogi and 16 thousand in Go. Stockfish examined about 70 million per second and Elmo about 35 million.
So AlphaZero used roughly a thousand times fewer evaluations in chess, each more informed.

To compare results we turn a match score s into an Elo difference. For the 2017 match, s is 64 percent, about 100 Elo. For the 2018 match, 155 wins, 839 draws and 6 losses give s about 57.5 percent and a difference of about 52 Elo.
Elo is only meaningful for the conditions of the match, and small score differences can be noise in small samples.

The criticism. After the preprint, commentators noted that the first match gave Stockfish little hash memory, a fixed time per move that denied its time management, and no opening book or endgame tablebase, and that the hardware was not comparable.

DeepMind answered in the Science paper with 1000 games under conditions like the TCEC superfinal, on 44 threads and 32 GB of hash with tablebases, and also tried openings from human games and time-odds matches.
The result held, +155 -6 =839, and Stockfish needed about ten to one time odds to match AlphaZero, according to the reports.
Not everyone was convinced even then. The match was private and only a small share of the games were published.

The Stockfish used was a development build from January 2018, and some experts, including the chess engine developer Larry Kaufman, said a newer Stockfish would probably beat AlphaZero under TCEC conditions. Meanwhile AlphaZero was never released.
What survives is the algorithm, which open-source projects such as Leela Chess Zero reproduced.

A fair summary: the evidence that a general self-learning method can reach top-engine strength in a day is solid. Claims about exactly how much stronger it was depend on hardware and settings, and should be read with the conditions attached.

summary: The capstone is a working AlphaZero-style search for tic-tac-toe, with the network stubbed out: every legal move gets the same prior, and every non-terminal leaf has value zero.
What remains is the machinery of the previous chapters: tree, PUCT selection, expansion, backup with sign flips and terminal results from the rules.
Even with a know-nothing network, the search finds forced wins and blocks, because real results at terminal positions flow back up the tree. Visit counts concentrate on the right move.
A trained network would supply better priors and values and make the search reach further for the same number of simulations.

Simulation: select by PUCT, recurse on the child, back up the negated value.
Unknown leaf: create its node, return value 0 (the stub network).
Finished game: win = +1 for the player who moved last, seen as -1 by the mover now.

items: ELI5. The build puts the parts together at toy size: a small network, a search and a self-play loop. Seeing each piece working makes the big system feel less magical.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: how do the search and network call each other in the toy?

Time to put everything together. The capstone lab is a small version of the AlphaZero search for tic-tac-toe, with the neural network replaced by a stub. We keep everything else: the tree, the statistics on each edge, the PUCT rule, the backup with sign flips.

The stub network says two things about any position it is asked about. The policy is uniform over the legal moves, as an untrained network's would roughly be after masking. The value is zero, meaning no opinion. It knows nothing about tic-tac-toe, not even that three in a row wins.

The only real information comes from the rules. When a simulation reaches a position where the game is over, we do not ask the network: the rules say who won. If the last mover completed a line, the player to move at that position has lost, so the value there is minus one for them.
A drawn board is zero.

A simulation is a recursive function. It takes a position and the player to move. If the game is over, return the exact value. If the position is not in the tree yet, create its node, with uniform priors, and return zero.

Otherwise pick the move maximizing Q plus U, play it, call the simulation on the child with the other player, and negate the result. Update that edge's visit count and total, and return the negated value to the caller.

Why does negating work? The child's value is for the player to move at the child, who is the opponent. What is good for the opponent is bad for us. This is the same sign flip of chapter 5, written as a recursion.
Run it. At the root you have nine counters. Start with the position X X dot, O O dot dot dot dot, with X to move: X wins by playing square 2. Early simulations spread visits by the uniform prior.

As soon as one simulation plays square 2 the child is terminal, returns a win, and that edge's Q becomes high. PUCT keeps choosing it, and its visit count dominates. No knowledge of tic-tac-toe was needed, only the rules.
What the real network adds. A trained network would give the winning move a high prior from the start, and would rate quiet positions by their likely outcome, not zero.

The tree could then answer correctly with far fewer simulations, and would work in games like chess, where terminal positions are too far away to be reached by chance. That is the entire point of the network: it gives the search a sense of direction.

The app after this chapter's labs runs the same search in your browser. Change the number of simulations and the exploration constant and watch the visit counts, the mean values and the priors on each square.
Finally, remember the limits of the miniature. It has no learning at all. Chapter 12 describes what is missing from a full system, and where later research went.

chapters.title: Successors, limits and open questions

maps.title: Beyond AlphaZero

Gumbel variants | add | Policy improvement guarantee

summary: AlphaZero was not released, but its papers were detailed enough for the community to rebuild it. Leela Zero followed AlphaGo Zero for Go and Leela Chess Zero followed AlphaZero for chess, both powered by volunteers who donate computing time for self-play. KataGo and others extended the idea.
MuZero, also from DeepMind, drops the requirement that the rules are given: it learns a model of the environment and plans with it, so the same approach covers video games as well as board games.
Gumbel variants of AlphaZero and MuZero change the search to guarantee policy improvement even with few simulations.
The limits are real. AlphaZero needs a perfect and fast simulator of the game rules, perfect information, and a lot of compute. The strongest-claims about generality refer to this class of games.

keyPoints: Leela Zero (Go, from 2017) and Leela Chess Zero (chess, from 2018) reproduced the methods with volunteer compute.
By 2020 Lc0 had reached the strength of AlphaZero's published results, according to a University of Alberta paper.
MuZero does not need the rules; AlphaZero does.

items: ELI5. Later systems added planning with learned models and games with hidden information. Limits remain: it needs a simulator, lots of compute and clear rules.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what must a problem provide for AlphaZero to work?

What happened next? The AlphaZero papers described the algorithm well enough to build, and the community did. Leela Zero, released in October 2017 by Gian-Carlo Pascutto, was an almost exact replication of AlphaGo Zero for Go.
In early 2018 another team branched Leela Chess Zero from it, to verify the methods in the AlphaZero paper for chess.

Both are distributed efforts: volunteers run clients that generate self-play games on their own machines and upload them, while a server trains the network. The Leela Zero server was shut down in February 2021, pointing users to KataGo and SAI.
Leela Chess Zero kept going, and according to a 2021 University of Alberta paper surpassed AlphaZero's published playing strength in 2020.
MuZero is the main successor from DeepMind. AlphaZero is given the rules of the game, both to run the search and to score finished games.

MuZero removes that: it learns a model that predicts, from its own internal state, the next state, the reward and the policy and value, and does the tree search inside that learned model. That lets the family include Atari games, where the rules are not available as a program.
Gumbel AlphaZero and Gumbel MuZero. Research on how the search improves the policy noted that neither AlphaZero nor MuZero guarantees policy improvement unless all actions are evaluated at the root.
The Gumbel variants add Gumbel noise in the way actions are chosen at the root so that improvement is guaranteed, and they remain effective with very few simulations.

What AlphaZero cannot do. It needs a fast, exact simulator of the game, since the search runs thousands of simulated games per move. It assumes perfect information: both players see everything, which excludes poker or Stratego-like games without extensions.
It assumes two players with opposing goals, so the sign-flip backup applies. And it needs computing power: thousands of specialized chips in the published runs.

Open questions remain, and the literature raises them. How much of the result depends on the compute budget rather than the algorithm? How do these systems fail, for example on positions with a deep tactical trap or in long endgames, where studies of open-source reproductions compare their choices with tablebases? The Alberta studies find that even strong AlphaZero-style programs still make mistakes in endgames that tablebases solve exactly.

The ideas that last. A learned evaluation guiding search. Search as a source of better training targets than the network alone. Self-play as a source of unlimited data when the game can be simulated. These ideas carry over to other domains, though each transfer needs its own simulator and reward.

You have now built and run the parts. The final exam covers the whole course. A closing reminder of the honesty rules: numbers here come from the papers and reports named in chapter 1, the capstone is a teaching miniature, and claims about the strength of AlphaZero versus current engines depend on the conditions of each match.
